messages.subject_clean: Conditional vs full likelihood, ExpectedN vs RealisedN
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have two questions about secr and would be thankful if somebody could throw some light.

1) I have read about the differences in expected and realized N. I am running into issues as the area I am interested in estimating N over is way smaller than my state space so expected N is less than the minimum number of individuals I detected. Is it accurate to think about expected N as the number of individuals with home range centers in the area of interest while realized N is that plus accounts for individuals whose activity center is outside the area of interest but their home range partially overlaps with the area of interest, and they were detected on this particular realization of the process?

2) I am using camera trap data, and the sex of some of the individuals of my study species is unknown. I am running the hybrid mixture model (hcov=sex) to accommodate missing sex. Can I use either the conditional or maximum likelihood? I am having better luck with conditional but wanted to be sure both are valid. Also, I read about the four different ways to model sex differences of which the hybrid mixture model and CL=T are two, however, the tutorial mentions not to mix them if I needed to compare the models using AIC, but I have seen people using these two together ......secr.fit (Capt, CL=T, hcov="sex",...)

Thanks

Tashi

Hello
1. No, that would be a mistake. An appendix to my recent Ecology paper has the title "Realized population size in an arbitrary small region". That may help, but it's rather technical and doesn't really solve anything unless you have telemetry data. The main message is that to estimate the realised population in a small region A you need some way to partition the contribution of each detected animal between 'inside A' and 'outside A'.
2. Yes, use either CL = F or CL = T. Just don't compare AIC for these two methods, and if you use hcov = 'sex' (note quotes) then do it consistently, even with null models (g0~1, sigma~1). secr.fit (Capt, CL=T, hcov="sex",...) is quite OK.
Murray

messages.subject_clean: Unbiased estimate of populatiuon density in a sub-area
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

we are investigating a deer population in an area of interest A, and the goal is to estimate the population density within this area. We thus systematically covered A with camera traps, and we concentrate on individuals which can be identified by individual patterns (such as antlers) and thus can apply SECR. The home rages of these animals are relatively large relative to the camera trap density and to the extend of A. Furthermore, the area surrounding A is also used by deers, i.e., there are several home range centres outside A with home-ranges partially overlapping with A (see attached scheme).

After reading carefully the Efford & Fewster paper in Oikos (2013)  (especially Figure 1) as well as the literature related to the SECR-package I am still not sure which approach is appropriate:

(1) We could ignore the shape of A at the beginning but define the area of integration by a relatively wide buffer (respectively buffer width as estimated from the data) leading to a larger area B comprising A. This gives us an unbiased estimate of the number of animals with home ranges overlapping with at least one camera trap (red circles in the attached scheme). However, the animal density with respect to B should be underestimated here, since there are several home ranges not overlapping with a camera but with the outer regions of B (see attached scheme). Thus, we can't adopt this density for A as far as I see.

(2)  Instead we could force secr.fit() to restrict the area of interest to  A. However,  as far as I understand also these results would be biased, since some caught animals would have home-range centres outside A, but home ranges are forced to lie within A.

I would be very happy if somebody has an idea how to solve this.

Thank you very much in advance,

Moritz

messages.subject: Re: transect data input
messages.subject_clean: transect data input
messages.body_plain:
Hi

Input of transect data is the same as for polygon data. Do not confuse transects and occasions. If one transect was searched on your first occasion and another on the second occasion then you have two transects with incomplete usage. An example of usage coding is given for polygon data on p.8 of secr-datainput.pdf <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-datainput.pdf>. Following that example usage would be 10 for the transect(s) searched on the first occasion and 01 for the transect(s) searched on the second occasion. The ID number is the animal ID.

It's not a bad thing to have lots of data, unless there is a risk of non-independence (I can't offer any help there). It can be faster and simpler to model discretized data (see ?discretize). Be aware of the potential issues with linear arrays when home ranges might be aligned.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Melissa,

Murray can correct me if I give misleading advice, but I have been doing scat surveys on an island. What we do is have people record tracklogs of where they search for bobcat and coyote scat. When they find scat they record the x-y location.

Because multiple people walk the same transects (trails) we combine their routes into a single “transect”. We do this because there is invariably some GPS error in the tracklogs where you have to double-back, just plain GPS error, etc.

These consolidated tracklogs become routes so we can indicate how many times a route was covered (measure of effort). Then we discretize the routes into 200-m segments. Each segment is further discretized into a point detector.

Locations where we detected a scat are then “snapped” to the nearest transect “point”

The area we search is 15 mi long by 1/4 to 2 miles wide. The resulting error in coordinates is very small compared to the size of the home range of the bobcats.

Perhaps using the approach I outlined may address some of the problems that seem to be of concern in your emails? Although what I suggest may depend on the scale of your search effort relative to the home range size of rabbits.

Again, Murray might point out problems with my approach. I have tried transect and polygon approaches with my data and what I described seems the simplest, straightforward, and appears to work. You might be able to use your GPX points as detectors?

Regards,

Duane

messages.body_plain:
Sorry I wasn’t clear - the center of each 200-m section of a transect was designated a detector.

I agree a probability-based sampling design is best. But bobcats tend to deposit scats along trails and so we walk all trails and roads on the island. No idea how to search any other way and collect enough scats! The problem with the track-logs of where people walked is that they are not exactly identical even if they walked the exact same trail or road. It just made sense to identify a single transect from the track-logs and then assign effort based on the number of times the transect was searched.

Good luck Melissa!

Thank you Duane and Murray, I appreciate the input!

Murray, I cleaned up my transects and that did help with initial input (this probably wasn't the best patch to start with - track points on access paths should not have been recorded by techs). The design of this study is to survey a shrubland patch on two occasions, with transects winding throughout the patch spaced 30 m apart, picking up fecal samples every 30 m along a transect when scat is present.

I like the idea of breaking transects into shorter segments and then proximity detectors. I'm working on a much smaller scale for rabbits than bobcats, so I tried snipping transects into 20 m segments. That worked. When discretizing capture histories, however, I get null values.

I have three remaining questions: 1) what should I fix in my code for discretizing capture histories to avoid null values, 2) I do not need to use make.capthist if I am using discretize, correct?, 3) Have I properly addressed usage in read.traps (points on one transect were only searched in the first occasion, points on the other transect only searched in the second occasion; I am calling the whole search path for each occasion one transect).

Thank you, apologies for the learning curve. I am trying to make use of examples and documentation before asking questions. Below is my code and the current input files I'm working with.

# create trapfile and captfile
trapfile<- read.traps('wellsTrans3.txt', detector = 'transect', binary.usage = TRUE)
captfile <- read.table('WellsCapt4.txt')

# snip trapfile to shorter 20 m segments, snip captures to 5 m rasterized points
snip(trapfile, from = 0, by = 20)

# Questions on the below code:

# tried snip
CH <- snip (captfile, by=5)
# null values

# reduce capture histories from transect to proximity detectors (individuals can be captured more than once, fecal surveys)
CH <- reduce (CH, outputdetector = "proximity")
# error: Error in array(x, c(length(x), 1L), if (!is.null(names(x))) list(names(x),  : 'data' must be of a vector type, was 'NULL'

CHproximity <- discretize(CH, spacing = 5, outputdetector = "proximity")
# also null values?

# Do I not need make.capthist because I have done that with discretize? How do I snap capture points to a detector?
CH <- make.capthist(captfile, trapfile, fmt = 'XY', noccasions = 2, snapXY=TRUE)

# then I would fit the model
fit <- secr.fit(CH)

Best,

Melissa

Bayesian SMR fun-fact for those who are interested. When the density of marked individuals on the landscape is low, knowing the spatial location of the sample carries a lot of information about their individual identity, much more so than for the unmarked individuals who are typically more dense given typical marking rates. Jose Jimenez has a paper under review demonstrating this. If the density of marked individuals is low enough, it's possible that knowing the spatial location of marked but no identity samples effectively tells you who they are with certainty.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Probably a newbie related cause, but I have tried to run some simulations to decide on a detector layout, and R just never ends computing.

We are studying ground squirrels, and, from visual counts, we calculate around 300-400 individuals per hectare.

Each occasion is a day in the field, during which we constantly check 20 traps. They are single-catch, but as the animals are removed almost immediately and the traps reset, I guess "proximity" is more close to reality (?)

Last year we traped 81 individuals in 6 days, although the trap number and location varied slightly. I have used that information to guess lambda0 and sigma using this code:

grid <- make.grid(4, 5, detector = "proximity")
msk <- make.mask(grid, buffer = 100, type = 'trapbuffer')
getdetectpar(D = 300, C = 81, traps = grid, mask = msk, noccasions = 6)

$lambda0
[1] 0.4828987

$sigma
[1] 2.886751

Both literature and our own observations suggest that sigma should be much larger, so I've been using 30 in these simulations. I have basically recycled the code in the secrdesign-Enrm pdf. Initially, I wanted to select between 6 types of rectangular grids, using either 20 or 30 traps, but I've been reducing the potential models, trying to run faster. To no avail. Still waiting!

Any help? Thanks for reading!
The code:

# generate scenario dataframe
scen <- make.scenarios (trapsindex = 1:3, detectfn = 'HHN', D = c(370),
lambda0 = c(0.31), sigma = 30, noccasions =  8)

# detector layouts
traplist <- list(
grid4x5 = make.grid(4,5,  detector = 'proximity',spacing=10),
grid2x10 = make.grid(2,10,   detector = 'proximity',spacing=10),
grid3x7 = make.grid(3,7,   detector = 'proximity',spacing=10)
)

# deterministic summary: expected counts
nrm <- scenarioSummary(scen, traplist)
# stochastic simulations
sumnrm <- function(CH)
c(n = nrow(CH), r = sum(CH) - nrow(CH),
m = sum(unlist(secr::moves(CH))>0, na.rm = TRUE))

sim <- run.scenarios(scen, trapset = traplist, nrepl = 1000,
extractfn = sumnrm, fit = FALSE, ncores = 3)

Fernando

I cannot explain why this job would never end, but it is certainly going to take a long time. Your chosen parameters lead to >1000 individuals and >10000 captures, and you ask for 1000 replicates. It works in 0.15 minutes when I try with just 2 replicates, and there is essentially no difference among the layouts with respect to approximate RSE(D-hat). Of course this is with fit = FALSE.When I use the shortcut simulation method='none' with 5 replicates, secrdesignapp gives me usable results for RSE(D-hat) in about 30 seconds.

With sigma = 30 m and detectfn = 'HHN' none of your three array configurations spans a 95% home range and I predict your density estimates will be quite biased.

Note also that the "overlap" coefficient k takes the value 5.8. That is way more than anything I have seen, and implies extreme sociality. getdetectpar() defaults to k = 0.5, hence the discrepancy. There may be something unusual about these critters I don't fully understand. I think you need secure pilot data for actual lambda0 and sigma.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi group!

I  was curious, if anyone has any ideas regarding how you to incorporate information on marking success into a spatially-explicit capture-recapture model. I’m not sure there’s a way to do that using the SECR package, but maybe someone has a good lead to investigate?

We are working on setting hair snare corrals for black bear, and we are unsure if the hair snares are effective at marking cubs. After a pilot season this last summer, we decided on using clusters of hair snare corrals spread across our study area. We are planning to set 4 hair snare corrals per cluster, 3 with a single-strand of barbed wire at 45 cm and 1 using 2-strands of wire at 20 cm and 50 cm. We’ll use teeth from bears harvested in 2020 to see if the proportion of yearlings (cubs during the 2019 hair snaring spree) marked by hair snares matched the proportion in which we set single- and double-stranded sites (i.e., if cubs were equally marked, we would expect that 75% of the marked cubs would show up on the single-stranded sites and 25% at the double-stranded sites).  We’re doing this more for an assurance since past literature suggests that cubs should be marked, but if we do find that cubs are missing the wire in single-stranded sites, how could we revise our population estimate? It's more of a hypothetical-case as we don't have the data yet, but are there ways to revise a population estimate by incorporating that source of data? Or maybe we can't?

Thanks for any feedback!

Laura

Laura,

Just a few comments that may not directly address your question.  First, the probability of capturing a cub is not going to be independent of capturing the sow, which is problematic for most capture-recapture models. I think your point estimate will be ok (Murray can correct me if I’m wrong), but the variance will likely be underestimated.

Second, the home range size of females with cubs is going to be much different from a solitary female or a female with yearlings depending on the time of year (the younger the cubs the smaller the home range of mother with cubs). These differences in home range size could lead to heterogeneity in the sigma parameter (maybe secr is robust to this violation – not sure). I think the later in summer you can do the hair snaring the better.

Third, your trap spatial design leads me to question whether it could affect your estimate of sigma. If you place these corrals in clusters are you treating each corral as a single trap, or the cluster as a single trap? If the former, could that lead to underestimating sigma? If a bear is likely to visit multiple corrals in a cluster much more than multiple clusters your estimate of sigma could be underestimated.

Finally, have you considered trying to collect independent auxiliary data? If you can estimate the number of females via secr (N-hat-females) and have an independent estimate of the number of cubs per female (c-hat-per-female), you could estimate the number of cubs as N-hat-females x c-hat-per-female. You could use the delta method to get a measure of precision on this estimate assuming you obtain a SE for your per capita cubs estimate.

Regards,

Duane

messages.body_plain:
Hey Laura,
To me, a good sampling design intends to limit nuisance variability as much as possible. If there is some size/age related variability in detection, the design you're describing seems like it could be inducing an interaction between something that is relatively well known (the characteristics of the traps) and something that is unknown (the size or age of the bears leaving hair, unless you're also trying to do some sort of aging with telomeres or something). Without an individual covariate for size/age, I think you might be stuck with using a finite mixture or an individual random effect (and if certain parts of the population cannot ever be captured, you can't model this at all). I dunno, maybe simplifying the design is the easiest way to approach this.
You could try to get some more information about any sampling bias, maybe using cameras (images or video) to see you can observe anything that would suggest some sort of bias in hair deposition|visitation. Visitation and deposition could be decomposed in a modeling exercise (Ben Augustine just built some options to perform analyses like this into his package), but maybe at the least visual evidence gives you a better sense of how to define the population being sampled (all bears, adult bears, whatever).
Duane raises good points about non-independence in the detection of individual animals if there are cubs and sows moving around together (the little I've seen positive/negative dependence explored in simulation suggests relatively small negative bias either way, but?). One other thing to consider is that sampling siblings that are moving around together may put a little more pressure on the lab to do a good job at discriminating individual genotypes.
John
